articles.title: Scotland lose Jamie Ritchie and Elliot Millar Mills through injury
articles.summary: Glasgow Warriors flanker Jamie Ritchie and Newcastle Red Bulls prop Elliot Millar Mills drop out of Scotland's Nations Championship squad following picking up injuries for their clubs over the weekend.
articles.body:
Glasgow Warriors flanker Jamie Ritchie and Newcastle Red Bulls prop Elliot Millar Mills have dropped out of Scotland's Nations Championship squad after picking up injuries for their clubs over the weekend.

Uncapped Ollie Blyth-Lafferty, fellow Edinburgh prop D'arcy Rae and back-row clubmate Freddy Douglas have been called up as replacements.

Ritchie, who has 63 caps, joined Glasgow from Perpignan this summer. However, the 30-year-old only made his debut last month after being sidelined for the opening months of the season because of ankle and Achilles tendon issues.

He started in the 24-20 win away to Benetton. But he came off with a knee injury after only 10 minutes of Friday's 29-20 win over Lions that took Glasgow to the top of the United Rugby Championship.

Millar Mills lasted five minutes of Newcastle's 59-26 defeat away to Northampton Saints in England's Premiership before the 34-year-old suffered a leg injury that will delay hopes of adding to his 15 caps.

Meanwhile, Sale Sharks scrum-half Gus Warr, who already has two caps, will join up with the squad for training this week along with uncapped Glasgow back Josh McKay, who is continuing his rehab from a hamstring injury.

Scotland entertain New Zealand on Saturday, 7 November before hosting Australia eight days later, then Japan on 21 November.

articles.title: Shaun Edwards: England turned down my offer to join coaching staff
articles.summary: Decorated defence guru Shaun Edwards says his offer to work for England at the forthcoming World Cup was turned down by head coach Steve Borthwick.
articles.body:
Decorated defence guru Shaun Edwards says his offer to work for England at next year's Rugby World Cup was turned down by head coach Steve Borthwick.

Edwards, 60, left his post with France earlier this year and, after a short-term role with England's women's side, has signed up to work with Argentina until the end of the tournament.

"I had a good chat with Steve over the phone," Edwards told Rugby Union Weekly.

"I said to Steve he can make me assistant kit man and I'll be there, I'll be ready for work.

"He was very, very honest with me and I thanked him for that.

"He said he was happy with his staff and the way things have been going, and I respected him for that."

Edwards is one of the most successful defence coaches in the game, having won three Six Nations Grand Slams during a 12-year spell with Wales and then helping restore France as a global powerhouse - with three Six Nations titles secured on that side of the Channel.

He also won two Champions Cups and four English titles during his time with Wasps, initially as a defence coach before taking on the club's top job.

Edwards, who was a hugely successful rugby league star with Wigan and Great Britain in his playing days, has long been linked with England's men's side.

Approaches were made by the Rugby Football Union to bring him into their coaching pathway in 2006 and 2008, while chief executive Bill Sweeney had informal talks with Edwards in 2021 but opted against competing with France for his services.

Borthwick's backroom set-up is already set for Australia 2027, with Richard Wigglesworth overseeing defence, supported by Byron McGuigan and Joe El-Abd.

England have endured fluctuating form over the past two years, with a 12-Test winning streak ended by Scotland in February and followed by five successive defeats.

They most recently beat Fiji and Argentina and now face Australia, Japan, New Zealand and a Nations Championship play-off on successive weekends through November.

Edwards says that his brief experience with the Red Roses was eye-opening.

He was involved in the build-up to England's win over New Zealand at Allianz Stadium, in which the hosts lagged behind on possession and territory, making only seven 22m entries compared to the Black Ferns' 15.

However, Zoe Harrison's last-play try gave the hosts a memorable 26-19 victory.

"The team made 310 tackles against New Zealand and we only conceded 19 points. That is probably the biggest stat I've ever been involved with in my whole career," said Edwards.

"Normally if you go over 250 tackles, you lose because the other teams obviously had all the ball."

Edwards added that the performance was all the more remarkable to him because of the different pre-match atmosphere around the Red Roses, compared to men's teams he has coached in the past.

"The girls are very joyous on matchday whereas, as men, we've got our heads down almost like we're going to a slaughterhouse," he added.

"I was thinking afterwards that maybe that's the way to go - be a bit more relaxed before the match."

Edwards, who was linked with the vacant Fiji job secured by South African Jake White, added he is surprised that his experience has not yet led to a head coach role with a Test side.

He believes he was a strong contender to take over the Wales job from Warren Gatland when the New Zealander ended his first stint with the country in 2019.

Wales opted instead to appoint Scarlets coach Wayne Pivac.

"I thought I might have got the Wales job when Warren decided to leave, but then I went on to something which I'd always wanted to do - which is to help France," he said.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Steve Borthwick names England squad with Alex Mitchell ruled out
articles.summary: England head coach Steve Borthwick has named a 36-player squad for the upcoming Nations Championship; Alex Mitchell is not included after suffering an injury over the weekend; Fin Smith included in the squad despite missing training camp
articles.body:
England are set to face Australia at Allianz Stadium on November 8 in round four.

The squad, comprising 20 forwards and 16 backs, assembles at England's performance centre at Pennyhill Park on November 2.

Alex Mitchell is not in the squad after the scrum-half was forced off during Northampton's 28-14 win against Gloucester on Saturday.

Mitchell had to come off with just 21 minutes played due to a hamstring injury, walking down the Franklin's Gardens tunnel to be replaced by 20-year-old Jonny Weimann. An injury update is expected in due course.

Scrum halves Ben Spencer and Harry Randall are in the squad in Mitchell's absence.

Despite missing England's three-day training camp ahead of the series, Fin Smith is included in the squad.

"We're looking forward to getting back to Allianz Stadium for four important Test matches against top-level opposition," said Borthwick.

"These fixtures take on added significance this Autumn as they represent our final opportunity to face Southern Hemisphere opposition before next year's Rugby World Cup.

"Facing Australia next Sunday is an exciting challenge. They have played a significant amount of Test rugby in recent months, and we know the quality and experience they will bring."

articles.title: England: Ben Spencer and Harry Randall called up for Nations Championship
articles.summary: Ben Spencer and Harry Randall are named in England's squad for this month's Nations Championship after injury hits Alex Mitchell and Archie McParland.
articles.body:
Ben Spencer and Harry Randall have been named in England's squad for this month's Nations Championship after injury ruled Northampton nines Alex Mitchell and Archie McParland out of Sunday's match with Australia.

Mitchell pulled up with a hamstring issue in Saints' win over Gloucester on Saturday, while uncapped prospect McParland, 21, picked up a calf injury in last week's training camp.

McParland, who would have toured with England in July but for a severe cut to his leg in the Prem final win over Exeter, could still be in contention for England's matches against Japan and New Zealand on 14 and 21 November respectively.

Mitchell will have a scan on his hamstring on Monday to assess the extent of his injury and subsequent lay-off.

The 29-year-old has suffered three previous hamstring injuries already this year.

Leicester's Jack van Poortvliet, who started all three of England's summer Tests, seems set to continue as first-choice scrum-half.

England are facing a possible change at fly-half, with first-choice Fin Smith struggling with a calf problem and Marcus Smith and George Ford competing to deputise in his possible absence.

Elsewhere Saracens' Theo Dan has seen off competition from Nathan Jibulu, Jamie Blamire and Gabriel Oghre to secure the third hooker spot in the squad.

Dan comes in in place of Bath's Kepu Tuipulotu who, like McParland, picked up an injury during last week's three-day training camp.

Gloucester centre Seb Atkinson and Exeter wing Immanuel Feyi-Waboso are also included after successfully negotiating injury comebacks for their clubs this weekend.

Midfield is the area of most selection intrigue with Gloucester's Will Joseph, who won his solitary previous cap back in 2022, and Sale's Joe Marchant, who has returned to eligibility after three seasons playing in France, included.

Bath centre pair Ollie Lawrence and Max Ojomoh, who both starred in last autumn's clean sweep, are omitted and there is no space for 20-year-old Saracens wing Noah Caluori.

After the matches against Australia, Japan and New Zealand, England will play a fourth Test against an as-yet-undecided southern hemisphere opponent in the play-off finals weekend of the new Nations Championship format.

articles.title: England rugby: Shaun Edwards says Steve Borthwick turned down his offer to work with side at 2027 World Cup
articles.summary: Shaun Edwards told Steve Borthwick that he would be "assistant kit man" if required but England head coach happy with his current staff; Borthwick's side play Australia at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium on Sunday, before clashes with Japan and New Zealand across the next two weekends
articles.body:
Edwards ended a six-year spell with France - during which Les Bleus won three Six Nations, including back-to-back in 2025 and 2026 - earlier this year.

The 60-year-old worked with the England women's team on a short-term basis and has now moved onto Argentina's staff until the end of next year's World Cup, which runs across October and November.

Speaking to the BBC's Rugby Union Weekly podcast, Edwards said: "I had a good chat with Steve [Borthwick] over the phone. I said he can make me assistant kit man and I'll be there, I'll be ready for work.

"He was very, very honest with me and I thanked him for that. He said he was happy with his staff and the way things have been going, and I respected him for that."

Edwards was Wales' defence coach from 2008-2019, helping the side to three Six Nations Grand Slam triumphs, while his success in club rugby union includes two Champions Cups and four domestic titles at Wasps, first as defence coach and then head coach.

The former rugby league player has frequently been linked with the England set-up over the years but will not be joining for now at least, with Richard Wigglesworth currently in charge of defence.

Byron McGuigan, Joe El-Abd and Kevin Sinfield are other members of Borthwick's coaching staff.

England return to action in the Nations Championship on Sunday as they take on Australia at Twickenham's Allianz Stadium.

Borthwick's side go on to play Japan and New Zealand at the same venue on November 14 and November 21 respectively, before the finals weekend across November 27-29.

articles.title: Joe Schmidt: Former Ireland head coach still proving 'very bad at retiring' in Ulster role
articles.summary: Some seven years after supposedly retiring from coaching, Joe Schmidt still shows no sign of stepping away from rugby as he prepares for month-long stint in Ulster.
articles.body:
"I'm not sure how good a coach I am, but I know I'm very bad at retiring from coaching."

When last officially involved in Irish rugby, Joe Schmidt was apparently bringing the curtain down on one of the great coaching careers in ill-fitting fashion at the 2019 World Cup.

The decision to, in his own words, "finish coaching" had been flagged a year prior.

For a man who had legitimately changed the way Ireland were perceived in the rugby world, a 46-14 defeat by his native New Zealand in the quarter-finals felt no way to say goodbye to the game.

As it turned out, of course, it was no such thing.

Some seven years into "retirement", and the 61-year-old has since held various roles with World Rugby, the Blues, the All Blacks, Australia and, now, Ulster Rugby.

"I think anywhere that I have been, I've been involved with really good young men who are trying to improve what they deliver," he said.

"I'm just a schoolteacher, and I'm just still trying to teach people as best I can.

"That's irrespective of where I am at any particular time."

'Small steps' for Schmidt at Ulster - Best

'I played with his voice in my head' - Schmidt's influence on Ireland

Schmidt has an amazing eye for detail - Dermody

After serving as a selector and assistant with New Zealand and head coach of the Wallabies, Schmidt describes his current role with Ulster as one that is "more for the future than the present", with an official title of coach development advisor.

The "pretty flexible" arrangement in Belfast will see him spend this month offering support and guidance to coaches through all levels of the province's pathways before returning again in April for another stint.

In between, there will be remote work. With stories of his rugby obsession well-worn, it will surprise few that such study has already started in earnest, even during his downtime last week while working with Australia A in America.

Despite enjoying such successes with Leinster before taking the Ireland job in 2013, with one of his two Heineken Cup successes coming thanks to a thumping final victory over Ulster, he does not feel strange now being associated with a different province.

"It's funny, I'm just coaching, so it's often not about the tracksuit top [you're wearing]," he said.

"It's just about trying to do a good job, trying to develop understanding, improve technique, and that doesn't really change. I don't think I change.

"But it's doesn't feel foreign. I've spent plenty of time in this stadium. In fact, before this stadium was built [in 2014], I spent a fair bit of time in an old wooden one that was here. It's not something I'm uncomfortable with."

Indeed, it was in part those pre-existing relationships at what is now the Affidea Stadium that helped pave his way for the surprising switch.

Rory Best, Ireland skipper for some of Schmidt's best days in coaching, is now general manager at the province, while head coach Richie Murphy was part of the Kiwi's ticket with both Leinster and the national side.

"I think it builds trust," Schmidt said.

"I think [Best] trusts that I'll work hard and try to help people as best I can, and I trust that Bestie will make sure that I get to do as much as I can when I'm in the windows that I'm on deck.

"I've known Richie, coaching with him for 10 years, and that was part of why I was comfortable coming in and working on the pathway so that when [players] get handed to Richie, hopefully they're in a good place."

While Schmidt ruled himself out of a return to Leinster to replace Leo Cullen in July, he has not closed the door on going back to frontline coaching some time in the future.

"I don't really see too far in advance," he said.

"A lot of things that have happened insofar as coaching is concerned are just sliding doors where people have phoned up or come and seen me. Even when I was teaching at Tauranga Boys College and the CEO of Bay of Plenty came in and said, 'hey, would you be prepared to do the attack for the Bay of Plenty Steamers [in 2003]?' It wasn't something that I'd set out to do, so I've never really planned.

"I've just coached as best I can, tried to develop the best environment, and I've tried to learn along the way. And so those accumulated learnings, they're not answers, but they are experiences and ideas that can help build a coaching perspective and capacity in the people that are here in Ulster coaching in the pathway at the moment."

Still, given past form, few will really believe we have seen the last of Joe Schmidt the head coach.

Having had such key involvements with Ireland, New Zealand and Australia across the past 13 years, will he, for instance, really be content just watching next year's World Cup from afar?

"I'm hoping to be sitting in the stands," he laughed.

"I'll be supporting three teams, so I'm thinking that I'm going to have a good chance."

articles.title: El chip que escucha los golpes
articles.standfirst: Un protector bucal inteligente mide las fuerzas G en la cabeza de los jugadores y sirve de prevención para alertar de posibles conmociones. Es obligatorio en encuentros internacionales
articles.summary: Un protector bucal inteligente mide las fuerzas G en la cabeza de los jugadores y sirve de prevención para alertar de posibles conmociones. Es obligatorio en encuentros internacionales
articles.body: En diciembre de 2020, el bufete Rylands Laws presentó una demanda ante World Rugby y las federaciones inglesas y galesas en nombre de nueve exjugadores, entre ellos Alix Popham y Steve Thompson, cuyo caso era dramático: no recordaba haber ganado la Copa del Mundo de 2003 con Inglaterra. El litigio, que aún sigue su curso tras haberse añadido 800 jugadores, terminó de convencer a los dirigentes de que por una cuestión de salud, que nunca lo es como tal hasta que no aparece el dinero, tenían que considerar con eficacia la investigación en las conmociones en su deporte. Después de distintas propuestas, la federación internacional confió su destino al protector bucal inteligente, un mordedor con un chip del tamaño de una uña que se había probado en la Copa del Mundo femenina de 2021 y que fue desarrollado por una empresa de Minnesota que había trabajado con los Navy Seals para medir fuerzas contundentes en saltos en paracaidismo y entrenamientos de combate. La batalla, en esta ocasión, era reducir los riesgos de conmoción, que por ahora, según la estadística, han disminuido un 20 por ciento. “Aún queda”, advierte Manu Sillero, responsable del alto rendimiento de la Federación Española de Rugby. “pero el avance es evidente. Hasta ahora se controlaba con la imagen de revisión de vídeo o los GPS que llevan en la espalda, pero es verdad que su posicionamiento no arrojaba unos datos tan certeros en términos de la fuerza que tienen que soportar en la cabeza como los protectores en la boca”. Si los dispositivos que maneja World Rugby en directo para competiciones internacionales, donde ya es obligatorio, detectan una fuerza de 8G, al jugador se le obliga a pasar al final del partido un test de conmoción (HIA). Si no lo supera, deja de competir durante 10 ó 12 días. “Se trata de un chip que tiene un acelerómetro y un giroscospio, que permite cuantificar la intensidad de los golpeos”, explica Sillero. “Pero también es cierto que aún a veces se dan ‘falsos positivos’, jugadores que marcan esas aceleraciones en la cabeza sin que haya habido un contacto. Ya ocurría con los GPS en determinados cambios de dirección o en saltos o en aterrizajes. Se irá puliendo con el tiempo”. El proceso comienza en la recepción del protector. Cada jugador lo ajusta individualmente con su dentista. El sensor mide el movimiento de la cabeza, no de la mandíbula. Cuando se supera el umbral determinado, el dispositivo envía por conexión inalámbrica una alerta a un médico independiente situado en la banda, que puede decidir si el jugador debe salir a una evaluación. Además, todos esos datos almacenados se vuelcan en una tablet al final del partido para cada combinado. Cada protector se guarda en un estuche que lo carga y lo higieniza con luz ultravioleta. Los estuches permiten gestionar hasta 27 unidades a la vez. La preocupación de los científicos va más allá de la conmoción visible. Las investigaciones de la última década apuntan a que los impactos repetidos en la cabeza, incluso los que no provocan síntomas inmediatos, pueden acumularse a lo largo de una carrera y estar asociados a un mayor riesgo de enfermedades neurodegenerativas, entre ellas la encefalopatía traumática crónica (ETC). Esta última solo puede confirmarse mediante un análisis cerebral postmortem, y los expertos aún debaten cuánto influye cada tipo de golpe, cuál es el umbral de riesgo y qué papel juegan otros factores, como la genética o los años de exposición. Esa incertidumbre es precisamente lo que da valor a los nuevos sensores. Hasta ahora el rugby podía contar las conmociones diagnosticadas, pero no medir la carga total de golpes que soporta un jugador. “El trabajo de prevención es muy interesante”, insiste el español. “Ahora mismo en la competición doméstica no se usa, pero en un futuro para etapas formativas me parece súper útil. Cuando se haga en cadena, seguro que bajará el coste y pasará como con los cascos protectores en su día. Los técnicos que lo han conocido así lo entienden”. Sillero ya había investigado con los GPS en esa dirección. “Nuestra conclusión en el estudio nacional que hicimos es que el jugador tiene una muy buena sensibilidad en la percepción de los contactos. Les pedimos que cuantificasen fuerzas de 4, 6 y 8G y la correlación en el cuestionario era mayor que el propio GPS”. El objetivo final es prevenir, pero también crear una estructura informativa que pueda orientar cambios en los entrenamientos, en las técnicas de placaje e incluso en las reglas del juego. El índice de aciertos ya se sitúa en torno al 86 por ciento, aunque, explican, el protector no diagnostica una conmoción cerebral. Ahí sigue estando la figura del médico, que ahora maneja más datos. “Es una herramienta joven”, insiste el responsable español. Quizá su mayor aportación no sea lo que detecta hoy, sino lo que permitirá saber mañana. Por primera vez, el rugby acumula datos objetivos de miles de impactos reales, y de ellos dependerá que se endurezcan los límites de contacto en los entrenamientos, que se afinen las técnicas de placaje o que se modifiquen las reglas. Para jugadores como Thompson, que hoy convive con la pérdida de memoria, esa información llega tarde. Para quienes ahora se calzan el protector, y sobre todo para quienes empiezan a jugar, puede ser la diferencia entre un deporte que se limita a reaccionar al daño y uno que aprende a evitarlo.

articles.title: Nations Championship: How 'student of coaching' Felipe Contepomi took unexpected path to Argentina job
articles.summary: As former Leinster star Felipe Contepomi arrives back in Dublin to lead his Argentina team against Ireland in the Nations Championship on Friday night, BBC Sport NI looks at the coaching career of the man nicknamed 'Dr Phil'.
articles.body:
Back when Michael Cheika was Felipe Contepomi's head coach at Leinster two decades ago, did the former Argentina boss believe his immediate successor with the Pumas would go on to have such a successful post-playing career?

"No, I didn't," he says without missing a beat.

The pair overlapped for four seasons in Dublin, building towards the province's first Heineken Cup in 2009 before the fly-half departed for Toulon that summer having missed the final through injury.

At a time when he was keeping a young Johnny Sexton out of the 10 jersey, Contepomi was a talisman during what was a foundational spell in the club's history.

Conversely, it was such abundant talent that made Cheika doubt his then fly-half's future lay in coaching.

"He was obviously a highly-skilled player and you know what they say about some of the best players? They don't make the greatest coaches because they think everyone can do what they could do and they actually can't."

Thirteen years after their paths diverged, and after Contepomi had spent four seasons as Leinster's attack coach, Cheika was bringing his former player into the Pumas set-up as his assistant. What changed in the intervening years?

"Felipe is different, right?" says Cheika of the man who brings his Argentina team to face Ireland in Dublin on Friday night.

"He's come into coaching raw and has had to take a step back, go and self-reflect on how much he really wants to do that. He went to Leinster and learnt his craft properly there with some good coaches around him in a team and an environment that he felt absolutely comfortable in.

"He understood what he had to do to become a quality coach first up and then a head coach, which is different to just being a coach as well."

Live commentary on BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sport website and app

Cheika's successor at Leinster, Joe Schmidt, spent three seasons at the province between Contempomi's stints as a player and an assistant, but considers the former playmaker a "pretty good friend" from their time spent in opposing coaching boxes.

The pair went head-to-head in the Rugby Championships of 2024 and 2025 while Schmidt was in charge of Australia. Each won two of those four contests, although the most comprehensive victory was Argentina's 67–27 triumph in 2024.

The pair would often meet for a drink or coffee before those Tests with Schmidt echoing Cheika's assertion that Contempomi possesses an ability to use his past playing ability as a complement in his coaching.

"I'd have a really high opinion of Felipe as a master of playing the game, but as a student of coaching the game," said the former Ireland head coach.

"I think he blends the two to be a really good coach."

It should perhaps come as no surprise that Contempomi has shown such aptitude for study as a coach having split his time in Dublin between playing and working to become medical doctor.

Leaving the Royal College of Surgeons in Ireland with a Bachelor of Medicine degree in 2007 earned him the nickname 'Dr Phil' among Leinster supporters.

Former Leinster back Luke Fitzgerald, who describes Contepomi as still having a "folk-hero status" in Dublin, believes that blend of intellect and experience is a compelling combination.

"He's a great personality and obviously a super smart guy, as you can tell from being a qualified doctor too," said the 34-times capped Ireland international who was a Test Lion in 2009.

"You can see his CV is very well filled out on the experience side, and I think what is the X-factor for him is that little bit of creativity that we would have seen in his own game."

Contepomi succeeded Cheika after the 2023 World Cup and has authored wins over the likes of New Zealand, South Africa and the British and Irish Lions as head of the coaching ticket.

Starting their second block of Nations Championship fixtures against Ireland in the Aviva Stadium on Friday offers the chance for another big scalp.

But he arrives back in Dublin amid reports , external he ruled himself out of the succeeding Leo Cullen at Leinster following the conclusion of his current contract with Argentina following next year's World Cup.

Contepomi's Leinster connection, coupled with a coaching CV boasting Test rugby success, naturally led to the 49-year-old being touted as a leading option to replace his former team-mate in one of the premier jobs in club rugby.

The likes of Ronan O'Gara, Stuart Lancaster and Leinster's current senior coach Jacques Nienaber were all also linked to the vacancy that it has now been confirmed will be filled by Bordeaux-Begles' Irish attack coach Noel McNamara.

Irrespective of what the future holds, Cheika believes Contepomi is doing an under-rated job with the Pumas building towards next year's global showpiece in Australia.

Ranked eighth in the world, the side may have won only six of their 15 Tests since that famous win over the Lions in Dublin last year, but Cheika points to the differing constraints in the role when compared to other leading nations who have the benefit of a stronger domestic game and, as a result, less disparate playing bases.

"They're performing great, well above their weight," he said.

"People take it a little bit for granted with Argentina. Well, 'yeah, they're a great team' and all that, but these guys are performing with so much less access to resources than any of the other countries that are at the top.

"He's had to go back and I suppose teach himself how to do that and he's done it really, really well and that's why the team is able to achieve more consistency than it's ever probably had before.

"I'm very proud of him, obviously as a friend of mine, a former player of mine, and now a colleague from coaching as well and I hope that they can continue that movement all the way through to the World Cup of '27."

articles.title: Kalyn Ponga: New Zealand star returns to reserve list for World Cup semis after broken arm
articles.summary: New Zealand call Kalyn Ponga and Phoenix Crossland into their extended squad for their 2026 Rugby League World Cup semi-final against Tonga.
articles.body:
New Zealand have named Kalyn Ponga on the reserve list for their Rugby League World Cup semi-final against Tonga - just three weeks after he broke his forearm.

And hooker Phoenix Crossland has also been included on the reserve list after completing a four-match ban imposed for the tackle that ruled Nathan Cleary out of the World Cup.

Ponga suffered a broken arm on 15 October during the opening game of the tournament, which New Zealand lost to Australia in a thrilling encounter.

The full-back played on for around 20 minutes with the injury as Australia narrowly triumphed 24-22, before having to go for surgery .

But even at the time, head coach Stacey Jones expressed hope that Ponga would be fit for the final on 15 November if New Zealand got there.

Crossland, meanwhile, is back available after missing the entire group stage as he served his suspension.

The Newcastle Knights hooker was sent off for a 'hip-drop' tackle on Australia's Nathan Cleary while playing against Penrith Panthers in the NRL play-offs on 27 September.

It left Cleary with a compound fracture and dislocation to his left ankle, ruling him out of the World Cup on home soil.

Crossland - who apologised to Cleary - missed the NRL Grand Final, which the Knights lost to Sydney Roosters, and sat out all three of New Zealand's Group A matches.

As it stands, Crossland and Cleary would not play in Saturday's semi-final as reserves, but they could still be moved into the 19-man matchday squad later this week before the game against Tonga in Newcastle, New South Wales (09:05 GMT).

Tonga, who effectively eliminated England by beating them 30-12 in their opening game on 17 October, are unchanged from their final group match.

They finished top of Group B-C with a 20-18 win over Samoa, and will look to repeat their 2017 World Cup group-stage victory over New Zealand.

Reigning champions Australia face Samoa in Sydney on Sunday (09:05 GMT) in the other men's semi-final.

Australia's XIII is unchanged, with Reece Walsh continuing ahead of James Tedesco at full-back.

Samoa, whose narrow defeat by Tonga confirmed England's elimination, bring in Ronald Volkman at stand-off after losing Chanel Harris-Tavita to a hamstring injury.

Women's favourites Australia return to full strength

In the women's semi-finals, red-hot favourites Australia are back to full strength to face Fiji on Sydney on Sunday (06:45 GMT) after resting players for their final group game against Wales.

Jocelyn Kelleher, who starred in their 78-0 thrashing of England, returns at stand-off while props Millie Elliott and Simaima Taufa and hooker Olivia Higgins also return.

Tiana Penitani Gray returns after a foot injury and joins Shaylee Bent and Olivia Kernick in the back row, having missed last Sunday's 124-6 dismantling of Wales.

Maria Paseka returns on the wing after missing two games with a leg injury in the main team news for the islanders.

In Saturday's semi-final (06:45 GMT), New Zealand face Samoa, who eliminated England with a 24-6 win in Wollongong last Friday.

articles.title: Leinster Rugby: Noel McNamara to succeed Leo Cullen as head coach
articles.summary: Bordeaux Begles attack coach Noel McNamara will replace Leo Cullen as Leinster's head coach from next season, the Irish province announces.
articles.body:
Noel McNamara will replace Leo Cullen as Leinster's head coach from next season, the Irish province have announced.

Cullen said in June that he would leave his role at the end of the current campaign after a trophy-laden 12 years with Leinster.

McNamara is currently attack coach at Bordeaux Begles, who defeated Leinster in the Investec Champions Cup final last season.

The 43-year-old previously spent five years at Leinster in a number of roles, including Leinster 'A' head coach and as academy manager.

He joined the Sharks in South Africa in 2021 as attack and backs coach before taking on his current role with Bordeaux in 2023.

Since moving to France he has helped Bordeaux win consecutive Champions Cups and they have twice been runners-up in the Top 14.

In May, Leinster were second best as they struggled to deal with Bordeaux's McNamara-led attack in Bilbao, with the French side running out dominant 41-19 winners.

McNamara, who also coached Ireland to an Under-20s Six Nations Grand Slam in 2019, said that the job was "one of the most prestigious roles in world rugby".

"It is an honour to be given this responsibility," he said.

"We have a very exciting season ahead with UBB and I am fully focused on that before moving back to Leinster next summer."

Shane Nolan, Leinster's chief executive, said: "Noel has a long association with the club and emerged as our preferred candidate very early in the process.

"His transition into the role will be seamless and we look forward to welcoming him here next July after this season reaches its conclusion."

The IRFU's performance director David Humphreys said McNamara has a "deep understanding of Irish rugby".

"Noel brings a wealth of coaching experience, strong leadership qualities and a proven track record of developing players and coaching successful teams," Humphreys said.

"I'm looking forward to working with him to ensure Leinster's continued success, while supporting the development of players for the Ireland national team."

Since he took over in 2015, Cullen has led Leinster to six league titles and the Champions Cup in 2018, but his side subsequently lost five finals in the competition, including four in the past five years.

articles.title: Ollie Chessum: Leicester Tigers captain on why he signed a new deal
articles.summary: Ollie Chessum says he could not imagine playing for another club after extending his deal with Leicester Tigers.
articles.body:
Ollie Chessum says he could not imagine wearing anything but the Leicester Tigers badge on his chest when he agreed to extend his stay with his boyhood club.

The 26-year-old England and British and Irish Lions lock signed a new two-year deal last week, which is reportedly worth £500,000 a season. , external

He has featured 89 times for the East Midlands club since first emerging from the Tigers academy in August 2020.

"For me there was no question," Chessum told BBC Radio Leicester when asked about his decision to recommit to the club.

"I love playing for this club, this has been my club ever since I've known what rugby is about and for me it was as pure and simple as I couldn't see myself with another badge on my chest."

Chessum signs new two-year deal with Leicester

Listen to the Tigers Rugby Show on BBC Radio Leicester

Chessum is in his second season as Tigers' captain, although his campaign got off to a delayed start as he recovered from a foot injury.

He scored a try in his first appearance of the season, which was a heavy defeat at Pau in the European Champions Cup, but he has gone on to lead Leicester in back-to-back Prem wins against Northampton and Bristol that have sent Tigers top of the table.

"I've loved every minute of being captain and being able to lead this group," Chessum said.

"Leadership is one of those things that I liken it to golf; people say you never master it. And leadership is exactly the same - you are constantly looking for ways to improve.

"The leadership stuff is all well and good but Geoff [head coach Geoff Parling] makes it very clear to me that week in and week out my job as captain is to first and foremost to play well. I think I'm in the perfect environment for that - the coaches we have now are constantly driving us to get better as leaders and more importantly as rugby players as well."

articles.title: England rugby league: RFL backs Jon Wilkin's £30m community funding plea to Andy Burnham
articles.summary: The new head of English rugby league backs a call for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to approve a £30m community funding plan for the sport.
articles.body:
The new head of English rugby league has backed a call for Prime Minister Andy Burnham to approve a £30m five-year community funding plan for the sport.

Former England international Jon Wilkin has appealed directly to Burnham and Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy, both rugby league fans, to pledge government money to a rugby league-based social impact project.

Ian Nolan, the new chief executive of the Rugby Football League, has supported Wilkin's plea, issued on BBC Radio 5 Live on Monday.

Wilkin wants Burnham and Nandy to follow the lead of Australia's government, which in July announced it was committing A$250m (£130m) , external over 10 years to the Pacific Rugby League Partnership.

That initiative is designed to help create sporting, educational and employment opportunities in Papua New Guinea, Tonga, Samoa and Fiji, and is being led by the Australian Rugby League Commission - the sport's national governing body.

Wilkin has argued that a similar plan for the north of England would benefit deprived communities.

He said: "Australia has recognised rugby league's potential as a vehicle for social change, committing hundreds of millions to developing communities, especially across the Pacific. Why shouldn't Britain show the same ambition for the north?

"The infrastructure already exists, the clubs, the foundations, the school and community relationships are already well established. What's missing is a coordinated strategy and meaningful government investment.

"The ask would be simple: For the government to establish a £30m five-year Northern Rugby League social impact partnership, bringing together the RFL, professional clubs, community foundations, local authorities and government departments.

"The programme would target disadvantaged northern communities."

Nolan, a former Manchester United executive who took up his role with the RFL on 1 October, suggested the social benefits of such an initiative would be felt more quickly because rugby league clubs are already established in their communities.

"When the government normally invest in community hubs and new things to generate something, they tend to be brand new," he said. "And it's really difficult then to attract people to go there because it's a new habit, it's a new place.

"But rugby clubs are already established in the most deprived towns in the UK. And that's the difference. People already go there. Families already rely on them for even just moving around."

BBC Sport has contacted the Department for Culture, Media and Sport for comment.

The plan England's rugby league bosses hope avoids repeat of World Cup pain

The England team who can still win the Rugby League World Cup

'A big opportunity to start a new Ashes-type series'

Nolan announced on Sunday that the RFL will be consulting English rugby league greats to map out a future for the national game under an initiative it is calling One Game, One England.

There is an acknowledgement within the governing body that the sport needs reform from grass-roots level upwards to ensure players of a high enough quality are developed to ultimately benefit the national team.

England's men and women have both exited the Rugby League World Cup at the group stage in the past few days - the first time neither team have reached the tournament's final four.

Wilkin has been highly critical of the set-up of the English game, arguing that an overcrowded Super League calendar - and the resulting lack of a mid-season international window - was a factor in England's disappointing World Cup.

Nolan is seeking ways to give domestic players higher quality fixtures, potentially in the style of the International Origin series - staged between 2011 and 2013, in which England played an Exiles team of overseas Super League players - or the War of the Roses, a representative fixture between Lancashire and Yorkshire, last played in 2003.

"I think there's a big opportunity for us to start to think of new Ashes-type series that we could play against the likes of Australia and New Zealand or even against France, or even domestically," Nolan said.

"We've had flashes with War of the Roses and even the Exiles games. Although they might not be international games, they're actually of an international standard.

"I think what we've done is we've always innovated and come up with these formats, but then we haven't given them a chance to really grow legs like State of Origin has in Australia. So I'm hopeful that we can come up with some innovations."

The World Cup is 'meant to be a festival'

International rugby league as a whole is facing intense scrutiny at present, with the men's and women's calendar largely squeezed in at the end of the club season, in October and November.

Former England international Ryan Hall told BBC Radio 5 Live that the men's World Cup had suffered for being cut down from 16 to 10 teams this year - with Scotland, Ireland, Italy, Greece, Jamaica and Wales all missing out.

That decision was made after Australia stepped in to stage the tournament, which was postponed for a year when scheduled hosts France pulled out for financial reasons.

"I don't think it is a World Cup," Hall said. "The essence of any World Cup in any sport is that it's a festival of the sport.

"Compare it to the football World Cup. Curacao were one of the 48 teams in the World Cup.

"I'm not saying rugby league could get 48 teams in the World Cup because that's not achievable, but [they could] certainly [have] more than 10.

"It's meant to be a festival and showcasing everyone of all levels of different countries who's eligible to play."

Wilkin, meanwhile, suggested that international rugby league's exposure has suffered because of a lack of a free-to-air live television deal.

Premier Sports is showing all the World Cup matches live, with the BBC providing live radio coverage, along with online highlights and live text commentaries on selected games.

Rights were awarded by the International Rugby League, the sport's world governing body. Its chair Troy Grant told the iPaper last week , external that it made the decision to go with Premier because the BBC did not offer enough money, saying he was "disappointed that the BBC didn't stump up". No other free-to-air broadcaster made a suitable offer.

Wilkin said: "The BBC Sport mantra has gone from showing live sport to clipping up digital assets. It's a digital format now.

"And I suppose we're now trying to compete in a market for those scraps of digital content with every other football club in the country. And that is alarming, isn't it?

"The World Cup should have been on the BBC. There is no doubt in my mind as a public service broadcaster, this had so many reasons to be a slam dunk home run to be free to air on the BBC. It had to be."

A BBC spokesperson said: "We must make difficult choices to deliver the savings required while continuing to serve audiences as effectively as possible."

articles.title: Alex Mitchell: England scrum-half ruled out of Nations Championship
articles.summary: Scrum-half Alex Mitchell has been ruled out of the whole of England's Nations Championship after suffering his fourth hamstring injury of the year.
articles.body:
Scrum-half Alex Mitchell has been ruled out of the whole of England's Nations Championship after suffering his fourth hamstring injury of the year.

The Northampton pivot limped out of his club's Prem game with Gloucester last Saturday, and England confirmed he will play no part in the matches with Australia, Japan and New Zealand this month.

Meanwhile, fly-half Fin Smith took a limited part in training as he continues his recovery from a calf problem.

He took part, however, in running drills on arrival in camp, with England sources remaining optimistic about his chances of being fit for Sunday's showdown with the Wallabies.

But the news around Mitchell had been expected ever since he withdrew in the first half of Northampton's 28-14 victory over the Cherry and Whites.

The 29-year-old had already picked up three hamstring injuries through the course of 2026, and now faces a prolonged period out of action for club and country.

Bath's Ben Spencer and Bristol Bears' Harry Randall were called in as scrum-half options on Monday, with Leicester's Jack van Poortvliet - who started all three of England's summer Tests - the likely first-choice nine.

Northampton scrum-half Archie McParland, 21, was named in the initial training squad but has withdrawn with a calf injury.

Hooker Luke Cowan-Dickie and flanker Tom Curry both took part in modified training today at England's Bagshot base, but are expected to be fit for selection.

England boss Steve Borthwick will name his side to face Australia on Friday.

articles.title: 'Fully loaded' All Blacks out to preserve record against Scotland
articles.summary: Mike Blair says New Zealand are motivated by their undefeated record against the Scots going into their Murrayfield meeting.
articles.body:
New Zealand assistant Mike Blair says the All Blacks will come to Murrayfield "fully loaded" as they seek to preserve their unbeaten record against Scotland on Saturday.

With recent meetings between the sides decided by single-digit margins, Blair says there is a respect for the threat the Scots will pose in the Nations Championship meeting.

"When I played, New Zealand played their second-string team. They gave guys opportunity against us," he said.

"Times have changed from that. We're fully loaded. We're ready to go."

In 33 attempts and 121 years of trying, Scotland have never beaten the All Blacks, and as desperate as they are to end that barren run, New Zealand are just as keen to protect their unblemished record.

"It's really important," said Blair, who played 85 times for Scotland and was head coach of Edinburgh from 2021 to 2023.

"We've got a couple of long-standing records. The Eden Park record [the All Blacks have not lost a Test there since 1994], every time we play there, there's an extra edge to it because you don't want to be the team that loses that record. It's definitely a huge motivation.

"We're really proud of that record [against Scotland]. We know over the last four matches it's been close, so it's going to be a tough contest for sure."

Having worked under Scotland head coach Gregor Townsend with both Glasgow Warriors and Scotland, Blair retains a strong relationship with his former international team-mate.

"We've been in touch this week," Blair said. "When I was over after the fourth Test [against South Africa], I was over for a couple of weeks and caught up with them and make a point to do that.

"We're just a little bit more cagey around certain things, how we believe the game's developing now and what we can do, because obviously we're up against each other now and I think we play each other before the World Cup as well.

"You need to be aware of certain plays the opposition might do over shape, but you've really got to trust what you're trying to do. I certainly feel like that with attack, you'll make little tweaks in your detail depending on what the defence offer, but if we get our game right then we can impose ourselves.

"So there's a bit of inside knowledge but I don't think it carries a huge amount of weight."

Blair says the squad and staff are still coming to terms with the shock death of the All Blacks head of security, Logan Cadwallader.

Cadwallader passed away suddenly on Sunday following the squad's arrival in Edinburgh, with head coach Rennie saying "we are all devastated".

"It's been a tough couple of days," said Blair.

"Logan was a big part of the All Blacks for 10 years and very close with players and management and obviously a huge, huge shock and it's taken time to deal with."

articles.title: England rugby: Alex Mitchell ruled out of entire Nations Championship due to hamstring injury
articles.summary: Alex Mitchell sustained a hamstring injury during Northampton's 28-14 win against Gloucester on Saturday; it is the fourth hamstring injury the scrum-half has sustained this year
articles.body:
The British and Irish Lions scrum-half underwent a scan on Monday, with the results confirming he will miss all four of this month's Tests.

It is the fourth hamstring injury Mitchell has sustained in 2026, dealing another setback to the scrum-half, who had been expected to play a key role in England's matches against Australia, Japan and New Zealand, as well as the Nations Championship finals weekend from November 27-29.

Jack van Poortvliet is now likely to start in the No 9 jersey for England's clash against the Wallabies on Sunday at the Allianz Stadium, with either Ben Spencer or Harry Randall providing cover from the bench.

Mitchell's Northampton team-mate Fin Smith is facing a race against time to be fit for Sunday's match, as he battles his second calf problem of the year.

Head coach Steve Borthwick will give Smith until Wednesday to prove he can play, with George Ford and Marcus Smith on standby to step in at fly-half.

Archie McParland, another Northampton half-back who is struggling with a calf issue, could return against Japan or New Zealand, but Sam Underhill (biceps), Kepueli Tuipulotu (knee) and Benhard Janse van Rensburg (concussion) will miss the whole of the second phase of the Nations Championship.

articles.title: World Rugby: Scrum, foul play, TMO - what can we expect from refs this autumn?
articles.summary: World Rugby has laid out a vision of a safer and more continuous sport, but with a desire to "embrace the contest" around the breakdown and set-piece.
articles.body:
The number of tries in international rugby has rocketed from six to eight per match in the space of just two years as World Rugby looks to futureproof the game.

It has laid out a vision of a safer and more continuous sport, but with a desire to "embrace the contest" around the breakdown and set-piece.

As part of the manifesto, the sport's world governing body will ramp up fan engagement and has launched a study using biometric sensors to find out what excites and invigorates supporters during matches.

Before the return of the Nations Championship, the top 24 international head coaches met with World Rugby officials outside London to discuss how the game will look over the coming month.

According to World Rugby sources, the coaches highlighted a number of "grey areas"; for example the scrum and breakdown, deliberate knock-ons and foul play in the act of scoring.

However, the coaches were said to be broadly supportive with the number of tries and the increase in ball-in-play time across the international game, which referee insiders attribute to an increase in speed and a consistent approach to the breakdown from officials and players.

Other top referees believe there is now more fatigue in the game, with officials encouraged to form scrums and line-outs within 30 seconds - which has helped with space and scoring opportunities.

As well as a rise in the number of tries scored, the number of penalties kicked has dropped from 3.5 in 2024 to 1.5 in 2026. The data was collected from all Nations Championship and Nations Cup games in 2024, 2025, and 2026.

The day after the coaches summit, a wider group of World Rugby match officials met at a conference attended by BBC Sport. The refereeing of the scrum, foul play and the use of the Television Match Official (TMO) were all high on the agenda.

The scrum presentation was led by former Scotland and Wales coach Jonathan Humphreys, while feted Wales and British and Irish Lions boss Warren Gatland was also in attendance in his capacity as a World Rugby advisor.

Former Kiwi official Brendon Pickerill, who was part of the refereeing team for the 2023 World Cup semi-final, led on foul play and the role of the TMO.

England's Mitchell ruled out of Nations Championship

Listen to the latest Rugby Union Weekly podcast

Fixtures and standings as Nations Championship returns

Special focus will be put on the following areas this November:

Scrum: Both loosehead props must have their right shoulders out to encourage a fair and even contest. The hooker must have his brake foot grounded in the tunnel to ensure scrum stability.

TMO: Will only come in for "clear and obvious" decisions. They will intervene in a "short window of opportunity" or otherwise will leave calls to the on-field officials. The TMO's remit will largely revolve around foul play and try-scoring situations.

Foul play: Crackdown on "hip-drop" tackles, with the entry point for sanction a yellow card. This is where a defender grabs an opponent from the side or behind, swings or rotates around them, and drops their body weight directly on to the ball carrier's lower limbs.

Reinforcement of the law around tacklers dropping to their knees before making a tackle.

Red cards: As has been the case since its introduction, all offences around the tackle and breakdown deemed to reach a red-card threshold will result in a 20-minute red card. The Head Contact Process - the checklist officials use to sanction foul play - has been updated to include illegal acts at the breakdown.

A permanent red card is reserved for egregious acts of foul play away from the ball.

The Nations Championship returns on Friday, 6 November as Ireland host Argentina in Dublin, and the tournament culminates in a finals weekend at the Allianz Stadium in Twickenham at the end of the month.

On finals weekend, all matches apart from the showpiece will use a "golden point" scoring system to determine the winner if the teams are level after 80 minutes.

articles.title: Nations Championship: Wales defence coach Peter Murchie calls for vast improvement
articles.summary: Defence coach Peter Murchie wants a vast improvement in his area of the game when Wales host Japan on Saturday.
articles.body:
Defence coach Peter Murchie has called for a vast improvement in his area of the game when Wales resume their Nations Championship campaign on Saturday against Japan (16:40 GMT).

Murchie is preparing for his second campaign in charge of the defence after joining Steve Tandy's backroom staff from Japan side Kobelco Kobe Steelers.

In July, Wales defeated Fiji in Cardiff but lost to Argentina and South Africa, with the side missing more than 100 tackles and conceding 15 tries during the three games.

Murchie is expecting a lot more from the Welsh squad during the next month.

"From my side in the summer, we can be much better," said Murchie.

"I wasn't happy with the defence overall, there's much more in us and improvements to be made.

"We want to be extremely tough to break down and play against.

"The players are ambitious, they want to perform and defensively we want to be more consistent in our performances this November."

Murchie linked up with Wales after the conclusion of the Japanese Rugby League One season in June.

So having come into the backroom staff late for his first campaign, Murchie is hoping to make more of an impression.

"There is a much bigger lead-in than last time," said Murchie.

"We've got more of a complete coaching group and been able to debrief the summer properly and prepare.

"We have been out in the regions and it's been a good preparation to getting the boys into camp.

"We have had more time to build relationships and prepare this time around."

Murchie stated Wales must improve their win ratio having experienced only three victories in the 12-Test Tandy era so far.

Since November 2025, Wales have beaten Japan, Italy and Fiji and have lost the nine other internationals.

"We're here to win Test matches, we're not here to take part and we've spoken about that as a group," said Murchie.

"I'm not going to give you a number of wins.

"We're also looking for consistency in our performance in terms of delivery and performance in every game."

How will Wales fare on Nations Championship return?

Where are Wales internationals really made?

The Prem talents hunting Wales breakthroughs

Wales will face familiar opponents on Saturday when they play Japan for a fourth time in 16 months.

Following the 1-1 series draw in Japan in July 2025 , Wales won the game in Cardiff last November courtesy of a last-gasp Jarrod Evans penalty.

The hosts now have somebody in their coaching ranks who can give him some insight into a Japan national side coached by Eddie Jones.

"I've coached there last year, so know a bit about how they play and how they approach the game.

"During the last year or two, they've progressed and pushed numerous top teams close.

"We know the threats, the skills and pace, particularly the Japanese contingent, have which is what they pride themselves on.

"They've also got a big foreign contingent there who give them a different dimension, size and bulk, especially around the forward pack.

"It makes them a difficult proposition to play against and they've proven that in the Test matches they have performed against us.

"We respect them, they're well-coached and well-drilled, so we'll need to be at our best."

Murchie gave an insight into how Japan approach rugby.

"They are extremely hard workers with the way they're brought through high school nand university," said Murchie.

"They will train for three or four hours and it's no sweat off their back.

"They're used to extremely harsh training conditions and will run through brick walls for you.

"They are also very fit, skilful and throw the ball around."

After spending a year in Japan, Murchie outlined the differences of the Japan rugby culture.

"It's different to anywhere else in the world, the way they're taught and coached and it makes them makes a really interesting group of people to work with," said Murchie.

"I loved it, learned a lot and the rugby out there is completely different. You work for a company and I essentially I worked for a steel company.

"So you've got a real tie to them and you've got to learn as a coach to work with 38-year-olds, who have been there for 20 years, and Ardie Savea [New Zealand captain] in the same team."

articles.title: Noel McNamara: What will 'exciting' head coach bring to Leinster?
articles.summary: After Noel McNamara's appointment to replace Leo Cullen at Leinster from next year, Hugo Keenan believes he is an "exciting" head coach.
articles.body:
After much speculation, Noel McNamara has been handed the keys at Leinster to replace outgoing head coach Leo Cullen.

McNamara is currently attacking coach at Bordeaux Begles, and helped to mastermind a dominating victory over Leinster in the Investec Champions Cup final in May.

When he was announced, McNamara described the Leinster job as "one of the most prestigious roles in world rugby".

But what will the 43-year-old bring to the Irish province when he takes over next year?

Ireland full-back Hugo Keenen has a long-standing relationship with McNamara, which goes back to when he was playing for UCD in the All-Ireland League, and he said it was "great news".

McNamara to succeed Cullen as Leinster head coach

The pair would have more interactions at Leinster when McNamara was working at the province as academy manager and Leinster A's head coach.

After five years in Dublin, where he also coached Ireland's Under-20s to Grand Slam success in 2019, McNamara made the move to South Africa in 2021 to join the Sharks as attack and backs coach.

From there, he joined Bordeaux in 2023 and has helped the French side to back-to-back European titles.

Keenan, who is in Ireland camp ahead of November's Nations Championship matches, said it was "an exciting appointment".

"It's good to have him on board and I think that's the general feedback amongst the squad," Keenan said.

"I'm sure he's got a different perspective of things, by getting out of the building, going down to South Africa, challenging himself down there, and going so well and thriving at Bordeaux."

Speaking on the Ireland Rugby Social podcast, back rower Jack Conan added that McNamara's appointment will be "huge" for the team.

"It'll be good to have him back. I never really worked with him directly before, but a great man and rugby brain," he explained.

"The lads are very excited. I think change is good and hopefully he can elevate us and bring some success that he's had at Bordeaux and push us to a new level."

Leinster know first hand what a McNamara-led attack can do, which was evident in the Champions Cup final in May.

The Irish province had no answer to Bordeaux in Bilbao as the French outfit made it consecutive European crowns with a crushing 41-19 win.

After that win, McNamara told BBC Sport he had used golfer Rory McIlroy, who had not long won back-to-back at the Masters, as motivation for his players.

McNamara had also spoken about Leinster's character in bouncing back after so many defeats, and said "tough times create tough people".

"Obviously, we know what he's achieved at Bordeaux and he's been on the better side of a few results than us recently," Keenan added.

"You see what their backline and attacks have been producing, and I suppose that's his fingerprint on it.

"I'm excited to see what he has and to work with him. I think it's positive for me and everyone at Leinster."

Keenan added that the departing Cullen was "big boots to fill" after a trophy-laden 12 years with Leinster.

The former Ireland second row has led Leinster to six league titles and the Champions Cup in 2018, but his side subsequently lost five finals in the competition, including four in the past five years.

Keenan added that the fact McNamara knows the province will help him evolve the side.

"He knows the club itself and he's been through the ranks," Keenan added.

"I'd like to think he's got an ability to grow the club now and grow the way we play, but while keeping how we like to play and the Leinster identity as well, so I think that's important."

But for Keenan, there is one attribute that has stuck out that he believes will help McNamara shift from an attacking coach to head coach.

"His man-management and his presence in a room," the 30-year-old continued.

"I still remember it from the get-go, from when he was a head coach back in the day with how well he speaks.

"I'm sure that's the same again, and I've talked about the technical points on the backs and the attack that I think he can bring as well, so it's exciting."

articles.title: Clark Laidlaw: The Scot doing famous father proud in New Zealand
articles.summary: Clark Laidlaw, head coach at Super Rugby champions Hurricanes, has made a huge impact in New Zealand and would "welcome a conversation" about taking on the top job in Scotland.
articles.body:
A few weeks back, four Scots shot the breeze in New Zealand, a meeting of rugby intellects transplanted from Edinburgh, Inverness, Yetholm and Jedburgh - all of them doing great things in their adopted land.

Mike Blair was one of them. On Saturday, in what promises to be a surreal day for him, the former Scotland captain will return to Murrayfield as attack coach for the All Blacks.

Euan Mackintosh was another. Mackintosh is the All Blacks' skills acquisition coach. The third man was Adam Hay, who is New Zealand's performance scientist.

The fourth was Clark Laidlaw, son of the great Roy, cousin of Greig and Super Rugby champion coach in 2026.

"We were getting a bit of stick at lunch, the four of us talking Scottish," says Laidlaw, whose Hurricanes team not only won Super Rugby in late June, they dominated it.

Finishing top of the table when the regular season ended, they won their first knockout game 66-12 against the Brumbies, then beat the Blues 57-21 in the semi-final before dismantling the Chiefs 60-5 in the final.

It was Laidlaw's third season in charge. He's far more celebrated in New Zealand than he is at home.

He's been there for 18 years, on and off, and he spoke about his life and times on the BBC's Scotland Rugby Podcast , how he went from a school-leaver at 16 to a New Zealand sevens coach - Commonwealth Games gold, World Cup Sevens gold, Olympics silver in Tokyo - to winning the ultimate club prize in southern hemisphere rugby in the summer.

Podcast: The remarkable rise of Clark Laidlaw

'Fully loaded' All Blacks out to preserve Scotland record

Scotland lose Ritchie and Millar Mills through injury

Eight of Laidlaw's Hurricanes players are in Dave Rennie's touring squad and it might have been double figures had injury not taken a number of others out of the reckoning.

Laidlaw is a New Zealand passport holder now, but he'll be on Scotland's side on Saturday.

"You're gonna see New Zealand's strongest possible team, but there's no reason why Scotland can't win," he reckons. "It's been a bounce of the ball here and there [in recent games].

"Scotland are definitely knocking on the door. I want Scotland to beat the All Blacks and I want the All Blacks to win every other game."

He was 30 when he left Scotland for Taranaki, as a skills coach on the north island. Given his upbringing he always had a curiosity in him. His father always spoke about being a student of the game.

"I just thought there must be different ways to look at the game and different ways to look at life, really," he explains.

"I used to go and pass my rugby ball against a tree at lunchtime and train at night. I used to say to the old boys, I wasn't going to be staying here.

"They'd be like, 'Yeah, you'll be here'. I just knew I didn't want to be there for 20 years. It's not like I had a bad life in Scotland.

"I had a great job at East Lothian Council and I was coaching Jed-Forest. But I was curious to see what was outside of those big walls in Jed."

New Zealand has changed him, he says. Not just as a rugby man, but as a husband and father. The Maori and Pacific Island culture has influenced him in a substantial way, knocking some rough edges off his personality.

"Being around so many different people from different backgrounds took a little bit of my aggressive Scottish side off me," he says.

"Not too much, I hope. I have more empathy and more of an understanding side and I certainly didn't have that when I was younger."

That process started during his wildly successful years on the Sevens beat.

"The types of athletes we would bring in were often young, so it became an environment where we did have to look after each other," he says. "We had to look after young players.

"Mums and dads were sending their kids off to the Sevens. It was the first time they were leaving home. So we did have to have a caring element to that programme as well as driving them forward."

His time in New Zealand was interrupted by a brief spell at London Irish a decade ago. Around that time, he had opportunities to go to Leinster and Montpellier but he turned them down.

After two seasons, he was lured back to New Zealand - and his life really started to change.

All of this begs the question about his future. Is he a potential All Blacks head coach? Would he welcome a conversation about taking over from Gregor Townsend after the World Cup?

He thinks Kiwis are open-minded on coaches who they feel can help them win. Himself and Blair are proof of that.

The Scotland gig is more immediate, of course. "Gregor's done an amazing job," he answers. "Lots of coaches around the world will be looking at that job with real excitement for whenever Gregor moves on.

"I'd welcome a conversation. It would be a lot to up sticks and move back to Scotland, but you never know in sport.

"One thing I have learned is you can't plan. My focus is on the Hurricanes. If that leads to international rugby somewhere one day then I would definitely look at it, but looking too far ahead can trip you up."

He speaks about his dad, how proud he is of him and also of the pain of seeing him living with dementia.

In eight years as a Test player - courage and class in equal measure in the number nine jersey - Roy got 47 Scotland caps and four Lions caps. "That would be 120 games nowadays, wouldn't it," says his son.

"How is he? The short answer is he's doing as good as he can. He's safe and healthy. He's in a care home in Jed and is well looked after.

"The family is amazing. Greig's mum and dad are amazing. My middle brother lives close by and I feel for him because it's tough on him.

"John Rutherford and Keith Robertson [his fellow 1984 Grand Slam winners] go across every week and sit with him. It's one of the hardest things about being on this side of the world.

"It's always in the back of your head that Scotland is home and moving back at some stage might be an option."

Deep down, you hope Roy knows the heights his son has reached in the game and what a massive part he played in it all.

It's been some journey so far - and you sense there are many more adventures to come, at home or in his home from home.

articles.title: Fin Smith: England hope fly-half can prove fitness ahead of Australia match in Nations Championship
articles.summary: England are optimistic Fin Smith will be fit to play in their Nations Championship match against Australia on Sunday; Smith has not trained with the international team since injuring his calf while playing for Northampton in October
articles.body:
The fly-half is to train alongside his international team-mates for the first time since injuring his calf in Northampton's defeat by Leicester on October 24.

England are increasingly optimistic the British and Irish Lion will prove he is ready for Sunday's Nations Championship match given he has progressed through every stage of his recovery so far.

Head coach Steve Borthwick names his team on Friday, potentially giving his first-choice fly-half two full training sessions ahead of his hoped-for comeback in the first of four Tests this month.

If Smith fails to get the green light, Test centurion George Ford and Harlequins ringmaster Marcus Smith will compete for the No 10 jersey in a duel between experience and form.

"Fin is really good and he's tracking nicely," Smith's Northampton team-mate Tommy Freeman said.

"He's doing the right stuff with the physios. It's always good having him there because of the connection I have with him at the club, which will always be beneficial for me."

Whoever features against Australia, they will partner Jack van Poortvliet at half-back as England reel from the loss of Alex Mitchell for the entire campaign.

A scan has revealed Mitchell's fourth hamstring issue of 2026 - a grim succession of injuries affecting both legs - requires weeks of rehabilitation, ruling him out of the Tests against Australia, Japan and New Zealand as well as finals weekend.

It occurred during Northampton's 28-14 win against Gloucester on Saturday and with another Saints scrum-half, Archie McParland, out for at least the Australia game because of a calf issue, England have been forced to add Ben Spencer and Harry Randall to their squad.

"To see Mitch go off like that is not nice, but these things happen," Freeman said.

"It's sport, it comes with the game. We're gutted for Mitch and hopefully it's a good recovery for him."

Freeman is likely set to feature on the wing, having started there for England's last two Test wins against Fiji and Argentina during the first phase of the Nations Championship in July.

The Lions star began the southern hemisphere leg of the competition at outside centre in the game with South Africa, his sixth consecutive Test start in the midfield, but England appear to have shelved experimenting with his position, at least for now.

"The wing's been a bit of a focus," Freeman said. "Playing there and having that continuity there is probably where I'm very comfortable.

"But I'll always have the ability to go into midfield if needs be. You see across a number of teams there are players who have the ability to cover positions.

articles.title: Rugby League World Cup: Can Tonga and Samoa create history with semi-final wins?
articles.summary: England were knocked out of the Rugby League World Cup thanks to disrupters Tonga and Samoa; Tonga will play New Zealand in the last four while Samoa face Australia in a repeat of the 2022 final; if Samoa beat Australia, will be first final without them since 1954
articles.body:
Tonga beat Samoa 20-18 in the final group match in an electrifying battle between the two nations that have grown into rugby league forces over the last decade.

The fixture was truly a sight to behold with fans out in force and the atmosphere dialled up to a level we have never quite seen.

A change in eligibility rules enabled a contingent of Australian and New Zealand-born stars to pledge their allegiance to Tonga and Samoa as they decided to represent their family lineage, the State of Origin eligibility being expanded only helping to grow their cause.

It has meant that, for the big three of Australia, New Zealand, and England, two disrupters have arrived. And disrupt they have.

England were dealt a tough hand in the World Cup, there is no denying that. But in years gone by, beating Tonga would have been a formality. Now it is a huge challenge.

That is thanks to head coach Kristian Woolf and his service to the side plus the players over the years who have battled hard for Tonga. They are reaping the rewards.

Similarly with Samoa, in the last World Cup they managed to overcome an opening-round hammering by England to break their hearts and beat them in the semis.

England will review how the World Cup unfolded with head coach Brian McDermott looking to stay on after being given just three weeks and tricky circumstances to guide his side.

But if England want to be in the mix internationally once more, they need to be backed domestically.

Without evolution, England's stagnancy on their investment into the international team has been laid bare and change will be long, tricky, and intricate.

They, effectively, need to try and become the disrupters to the teams that have disrupted them. That requires international competitions, camps, Tests, and progress to be the priority and not the afterthought.

Some of the greatest players in England's modern history will convene to help map out a future for the national game, including further analysis of the pyramid, from grassroots and pathways to the player pool for the international stage- they have a lot of work on their hands.

Since the first year of the Rugby League World Cup in 1954, there has been a clear trend. Yes, France took on Great Britain in that final, but then it all changed.

For the 15 finals that have followed, Australia have been involved in every single one and won 12 of them with New Zealand winning one and Great Britain or England winning in 1954, 1960, and 1972.

Samoa changed the narrative in 2021 when they stunned England in the semi-finals to make their first final. Now Tonga can add to that history too. They play New Zealand in the last four while Samoa will face Australia in a repeat of the 2022 final.

If they both win, a historic moment will unfold. If even just Samoa win, we will have our first Rugby League World Cup final without Australia since 1954.

If we see the Sipi Tau against the Siva Tau in the biggest final in the sport, expect emotions, fireworks, a moment to remember.

Lots of the players who chose to represent Tonga and Samoa made a huge call. They decided to go against the status quo.

Now, there is a world in which Australia and New Zealand are sat at home watching as these two teams do battle in a final.

Even if it is one of them - if one of Tonga or Samoa win the Rugby League World Cup, expect to see scenes of celebration like you have never seen before.

Tonga has a population of around 100,000. Samoa has a population of approximately 200,000.

But the shockwaves a victory for either would produce would be uncalculable.
