articles.title: 2026 Rugby League World Cup: Why sport needs Tonga-Samoa men's final
articles.summary: Tonga will face New Zealand after winning all three group matches, before Samoa face Australia in a repeat of the 2022 final.
articles.body:
With blow out wins and a convoluted format, the men's group stage at the 2026 Rugby League World Cup did little to dissuade cynics about the unhealthy state of the international game.

From Group A, Australia and New Zealand came through as expected and are widely tipped to face off in the final on 15 November.

But from the strange lands of Group B-C, two beacons of hope have emerged. Tonga will face New Zealand after winning all three group matches, before Samoa face Australia in a repeat of the 2022 final.

And if either goes all the way, it would be good for international rugby league, shaking up the game in the same way Wakefield's Grand Final win has for the Super League – proving there is still room for surprises in rugby league.

"Could this be a dress rehearsal for the final? I hope so," former Bradford Bulls head coach Matthew Elliott told BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra after Tonga and Samoa's riveting Group B-C match, won 20-18 by the Tongans . "I shouldn't say that out loud as an Aussie but I hope so."

History suggests this scenario is unlikely, but not impossible.

The first semi-final, New Zealand v Tonga, is a match with a dramatic recent history. Tonga beat New Zealand 25-14 in an epic Pacific Championships match two years ago to reach their first-ever elite tournament final.

Last year, their meeting was overshadowed by a head injury to Tonga back-rower Eli Katoa, who needed emergency brain surgery after receiving three separate concussions and has not played since.

Tonga were semi-finalists in 2017, winning their group after stunning New Zealand 28-22 in the group stage. In the last four they were only narrowly defeated by England, 20-18, scoring three tries in the final seven minutes to give the English a huge fright in their best previous World Cup effort.

Australia, Papua New Guinea, New Zealand

Listen to live commentary on every men's match, and key women's matches - with coverage on BBC Radio 5 Live, BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app

Samoa have gone one further of course and were surprise runners-up four years ago having not previously gone beyond the quarter-finals since first appearing at the World Cup in 1995.

They were beaten 60-6 by England in their opener but fought through to the semi-finals, where they stunned the hosts 27-26 in a golden point win at Emirates Stadium.

At Old Trafford they were overpowered by Australia but not overawed, losing 30-10 . In doing so Samoa became only the sixth different team to reach a men's final after Australia, New Zealand, Great Britain, England and France, in 16 editions.

Australia have won 10 of the last 11 World Cups, including the last three, with New Zealand winning the other.

Such dominance at the supposed peak of the sport, in a tournament reduced from 16 to 10 teams this year, indicates a gap growing between haves and have nots.

Of the outsiders, Samoa and Tonga can shake that up.

The teams met at the quarter-final stage of the last Rugby League World Cup, with Samoa winning a classic 20-18 in Warrington. Tonga won by the same scoreline three days ago, in similarly exhilarating fashion.

"The occasion was unbelievable," Samoa head coach Ben Gardiner said after the game. "I looked down at the start of the game and I've never seen so many people on the sidelines at a footy match in my life.

"It was a sensational occasion, and international rugby league is about that. It's about fanfare and it's about creating opportunities for our fans to come and watch our nations play. It was an absolute cracker."

Not only are the Pacific islands bringing the colour and passion of their nations to the world stage, they are also bringing world-class quality.

Nine players featuring in the group game squads played some part in this year's State of Origin, an annual series between New South Wales and Queensland representative teams regarded as one of the pinnacles of world rugby league.

"I think that was about five or 10 levels above NRL tonight," Tonga half-back Isaiya Katoa told Premier Sports of the group match. "Every tackle felt like the first of the game. There are going to be some sore bodies out there.

"Something that goes so unnoticed is the impact Woolfy [Kristian Woolf] has as the coach. He cares about every single one of us. The reason you've got Jojo Fifita and Rob Toia [two of the State of Origin players] wanting to play for Tonga is because of the coach."

Both nations have Australians in charge. Gardiner has been in post since 2023, while Woolf has led Tonga since 2014 and overseen their remarkable rise in rugby league prominence.

Both have experience coaching in the NRL, and have brought the quality and professionalism of the world's best domestic league to bear fruit on their respective islands – with both talking about working on "emotional regulation" in big games.

They have also both been helped by an international eligibility system which is much more forgiving to smaller nations than in many other sports.

Since 2016, the IRL introduced a tier system for member nations: Australia, New Zealand and England are in tier one; all other full members are in tier two.

Under this system, players can elect to represent both a tier one and two nation but are permitted to represent only one nation in a calendar year or at a Rugby League World Cup.

This flexibility has allowed members of diaspora populations to represent their family heritage and national identities – particularly those with ancestors from Pacific islands, who may have had to move away in the past.

These connections mean that when those with Tongan and Samoan heritage do represent their historic countries, they do so with gusto.

"I can't put it into words," Tonga prop Addin Fonua-Blake told BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra. "This is the pinnacle for me. Representing my people is something special.

"I just want to thank from the bottom of my heart all the supporters. You could feel it this whole week, the amount of support that we had, that both teams had. And it's only going to keep growing. What the supporters have done for this game, it's unheard of.

"A few years ago, we wouldn't even sell out a game out of Campbelltown and now we're sitting here on one of the biggest stages selling out, and it's only going to get bigger."

Both countries have also benefited from generous financial deals the likes of which English rugby league supporters want introduced for their team.

Australia's government in July announced , external it was committing A$250m (£130m) over 10 years to the Pacific Rugby League Partnership, designed to help create opportunities in Papua New Guinea, Tonga, Samoa and Fiji, and is being led by the Australian Rugby League Commission.

It is the kind of diversification rugby league badly needs, after a reduced and unbalanced World Cup which at times has struggled to live up to its name.

"The branding of the World Cup, I think that's wrong," former England international Ryan Hall told BBC Radio 5 Live. "The essence of any World Cup in any sport is, it's a festival of the sport.

"I'm not saying Rugby League could get 48 teams in the World Cup because that's not achievable, but certainly more than 10. It's meant to be a festival and showcasing to everyone of all levels of different countries who's eligible to play, get it out there.

"I'll talk about Italy in 2013. Italy don't play Rugby League too much. They managed to get a team full of people who love their heritage, based in the NRL, a lot of Australians, and they managed to beat England in a warm-up game. So don't tell me there's no countries out there, such as Italy, who cannot live up to displaying well in the World Cup and putting on an event."

If rugby league is to grow and the World Cup is to survive, it needs new blood to thrive. A world title for Tonga and Samoa would certainly help.

articles.title: Social media abuse, stalking and death threats: Why it's never just about performance for our sportswomen
articles.summary: Sky Sports News documentary 'Beyond The Noise' explores challenges our sportswomen face in pursuit of glory; Warning: contains discussion of social media abuse, stalking and death threats which some may find distressing
articles.body:
Who would be a sportswoman in today's landscape? In the eyes of some so-called fans, they can't do right for doing wrong.

In 2025, women's sport took huge strides on the pitch again as the Lionesses created another piece of history by defending their Euros title and the Red Roses claimed World Cup glory on home soil - as well as a host of individual successes from Beau Greaves' heroics on the oche to Lottie Woad's emergence on the golf course.

Yet many of our sportswomen are climbing their sporting ladders while being subjected to unsavoury comments and negativities outside of their sporting arenas. It's another layer of pressure for our athletes.

When Wales and Saracens' Georgia Evans found herself the subject of unnecessary abuse during the Women's Rugby World Cup last autumn for simply choosing to wear bows in her hair on the pitch, she took matters into her own hands. She couldn't stay quiet.

"There was a social media post [from another account] saying 'Georgia Evans is ready' [ahead of Wales' World Cup opener] and a picture of me looking quite crazy with two big pink bows in my hair, which isn't abnormal for myself," Evans told Sky Sports .

"But then I went through the comments and there were a lot of derogatory remarks regarding my appearance, how silly and childish I looked. There were a number of other derogatory comments and, while I didn't take them too personally, my team-mates and family were seeing them.

"My sisters were having Facebook wars with people for days afterwards arguing with women and men who were talking about how my parents had affected how we were playing, which was bizarre to me because I've worn bows in my hair for years. I've worn them since my first cap and it's never had a bearing on my ability on the pitch, to nit-pick on that was very strange."

'What I look like has no bearing on my ability'

Evans, who won her 50th cap for Wales in a WXV match against the USA in September, thought long and hard about whether to respond to the abuse, rewriting a statement "1,000 times over" before deciding to press send.

Within her response, Evans said: "This game allows space and room for every boy and girl, whatever their haircut, body shape or look they wish to wear on and off the field. 'It's not a rugby look' - a rugby player is no longer defined by your gender or what you look like.

'It's childish' - but to all those young girls it's understanding you don't have to compromise who you are to fit into a stereotype.

"In an old-school, man's game, I'm bringing a bit of Barbie to the party.

"To all those that aren't fans, that is OK. To all the support and love - thank you. Don't worry, I won't be changing."

Evans was blown away by the reaction on social media and the subsequent love and support she felt from the Welsh Rugby Union and wider rugby community.

Thousands of young girls, women and men turned up to Wales' next match sporting their own bows in a display of solidarity. A moment Evans will never forget, yet she feels it was a situation that shouldn't have happened. After all, why should sportswomen be judged for their appearance?

"People have a right to their opinion. As sportspeople, we put ourselves out there. When you're in the public eye, people will criticise you for what you do, which is what I do on the pitch. But what I look like, what I wear, how I choose to present myself has no bearing on my ability.

"A big thing that women find is you constantly just get knocked down and it's such a fight to get back up and be on the level playing field with our male counterparts. So when you're literally picking at someone's appearance, whether you are male or female, it's not what we're out here for.

"We're not models, we're not fashion models or icons in that sense but we're out here to do a job, so that was the important part for me, is 'criticise my rugby all you want' but hitting back at appearances is slightly too personal for me especially with everything that we do as women to put ourselves out there to make this game bigger."

Bartoli: I'm not sure next generation can survive that constant judgement

A survey by Women In Sport published earlier this year found the number of girls who dreamed of becoming professional athletes has fallen to its lowest level since 2020. Now just 23 per cent say they dream of sporting glory compared to 53 per cent of boys.

The research found that teenage girls don't feel that they belong in sport, feel judged and worry about not having the 'right' body as well as worrying about their safety. The report also revealed that 70 per cent avoided sport when girls are on their period.

Former Wimbledon champion, Sky Sports tennis pundit and coach Marion Bartoli is well aware of the alarming statistics.

Bartoli coaches teenage girls and has seen first hand the impact social media has had on their progress and future aspirations.

"I started coaching a girl when she was 13 years old, she's now 16 and I've seen her going through those three years with social media developing and how much it has affected her mentally with her body image and how much she's constantly looking at what people comment on her pictures or what people say about her," Bartoli told Sky Sports .

"I'm really worried for the next generation because it has come to a point where it is so bad - it is already - but if it keeps going I'm not sure the next generation will be able to survive that many comments and judgement constantly."

Bartoli knows how damaging a personal attack on your appearance can be to your mentality and confidence having infamously been humiliated in the aftermath of her 2013 Wimbledon triumph, the greatest success of her career, when BBC commentator John Inverdale made a derogatory remark.

"I've been criticised publicly on national TV after winning Wimbledon. Apparently I didn't look like Maria Sharapova but at the time it should have been more about me winning Wimbledon rather than how I looked, but yet someone on live TV made that comment. So I completely understand those girls who feel that everything is always constantly targeting one thing."

Bartoli, however, has been encouraged by how some of the leading players on the women's tour have been able to rise above the criticism by consistently being their authentic selves and not allowing the haters to win.

"I feel like you should express yourself the way you are," she said. "I'm happy to see Aryna Sabalenka with her massive personality. At the beginning, people were saying well she's too loud, she's too this, she's too that. At the end of the day, she's world No 1 and dominating women's tennis.

"She just signed with Gucci, so having a massive brand take her on board shows they want to have that kind of personality too.

"Coco Gauff said she was inspired by Serena and Venus because they were two black girls who could take on the top of the world of women's tennis and therefore she felt like she was looking like them and she could be there as well and she belonged.

"We want more diversity of personality, style, body shape, anything that makes someone feel more comfortable."

'Obsessive fans will break every rule to get to players'

But what happens when criticism about personal appearances turns into something even more sinister?

A report from the Women's Tennis Association [WTA] and International Tennis Federation [ITF] published last summer revealed 458 players were direct targets of abuse in 2024 while leading players including Britain's Katie Boulter, Elina Svitolina and Jessica Pegula among others have spoken of being sent death threats and explicit pictures by online trolls.

Most recently, Great Britain's Jodie Burrage also said she received death threats and abuse on social media after she was beaten in the first round of the Chennai Open.

The report found that 40 per cent of social media abuse came from frustrated gamblers.

Shockingly, at the Indian Wells tournament at the start of March, Italy's Lucrezia Stefanini revealed threats to her life sent to her on WhatsApp which included a photo of a gun ahead of a qualifying match.

"I received a WhatsApp message in which I was threatened over winning yesterday's match. They threatened me and my family and named my parents, the place where I was born, and they sent me a photo of a gun," Stefanini said.

It is not only disgruntled bettors that players encounter online but the physical presence of obsessive fans showing up in sporting arenas, with the sight of a distressed Emma Raducanu cowering behind the umpire's chair at the Dubai Tennis Championship last February due to a "fixated" man in the crowd, one of the most alarming incidents in women's sport in recent years.

Raducanu later spoke of how 'wary' she was to go out after the incident, with the man in question given a restraining order after approaching her in Dubai and following her from Singapore to Abu Dhabi and Qatar.

And is it any wonder that we question why a sportswoman has underperformed when there are all manner of off-court issues our athletes must try to put to one side as they pursue their ambitions?

Bartoli said that it sends "chills in my spine" to see and read the messages that players are being sent and is surprised that they are "ready to send those messages to a 14, 15, 16-year-old girl playing a junior event somewhere in the world" too.

It also brought back memories of her own stalking incident at Wimbledon where a man who pretended to be a groundsperson to get on the same court as her at the 2007 Championships.

"It was scary to see the level those people are ready to go to. I'd seen him follow me since all the grass court tournaments and he was literally right behind me throughout the whole match. I was 22 years old then, attempting to win my first Wimbledon.

"The club did a tremendous job making sure I was safe and gave me extra security for all my other matches. It was more when I thought about it afterwards, the fact you become an obsession for someone that they're ready to break every single rule to get to your court to follow you."

Major tournaments can lead to increased abuse

While major sporting tournaments have put our sportswomen on the map, they also have fuelled toxic conversations online.

A study by FIFA found that one in five players at the Women's World Cup in 2023 saw one in five players receive discriminatory, abusive or threatening messages.

And players at the tournament in Australia and New Zealand were 29 per cent more likely to be targeted than those at the 2022 men's World Cup.

A fresh study by Moonshoot, a UK-based threat monitoring service, found that during the 2025 European Championship final, 3,000 social media posts containing 'hostile or concerning content' were directed at the England team.

England's Jess Carter stepped back from social media ahead of the final due to a barrage of racist abuse throughout the tournament and earlier this year, a 60-year-old man who admitted sending abusive messages to the defender was sentenced to six weeks in prison, suspended for 12 months.

For Sophia Dunkley , who was part of England's T20 World Cup squad this summer that ran into an inspired Australia in the final, spoke ahead of the tournament about the importance of blocking out the noise.

"Over the last few years, as cricket has come more into the spotlight, it has definitely become a lot more prevalent [social media abuse], in terms of bad performances and bad comments," Dunkley told Sky Sports.

"We're switching on a lot more to how we can just have settings off, so that only the people we follow can comment, or by really making sure we have a close circle around us - and trusting the opinions that matter.

"Sometimes it's really easy to get carried away with thinking about what people think of us, but being really tight knit in our team really helps.

"It's definitely great for people to talk about it more, and normalise that, because it's a transition that women's sport is going through at the moment.

"Social media can definitely be a great tool - for your personal brand, for the team and to promote positive things.

"It's about getting the balance of those things, and also not letting it distract you from what you're trying to do."

Of course for some other sportswomen, they are not fazed by online hate they are subjected to and can ignore the opinions and judgements made by people hiding behind their keyboards.

Charley Hull has long fended off criticism for her actions on the golf course which includes a viral moment of her smoking cigarettes on course at the 2024 US Open.

Currently ranked No 4 in the world, and 10 top-10 finishes in majors - including runner-up at last year's AIG Women's Open - it is not her success that has got people talking online, more her outspoken nature, to which she gives short shrift.

"I don't really care what people think of me. I've always been like that. I've got my opinion, and everyone's in touch with their own opinion. So, honestly, that's just one thing I never really think of, and it doesn't bother me at all.

"I post what I want to post, and I just post those golfing videos as well because I enjoy it. And I just love the game of golf, so if some people don't like it, that's up to them. They're entitled to that, and if not, fair play.

"I just live myself, live my life the way I want to live it. I've always been like that. I do what I want to do, and if people don't like it, they don't like it. And I think a lot of people these days probably end up being unhappy because they always live in an image rather than being true to themselves, where I just want to be true to myself."

For all the momentum behind women's sport, the message from those living it and those closest to it is clear: success should not come at the cost of personal safety, mental wellbeing or identity. As athletes continue to push and perform under unprecedented visibility, the focus must shift from how sportswomen look or behave to what they achieve.

As Evans concludes, it's not about "pointing the finger" and telling people they are "wrong" but: "It's just important to know, we stand together as female athletes and we're not going to tolerate or put up with people saying personal things or people directly commenting on people's appearances, livelihood, how they go about themselves. When you cross that line, that's when we need to bind together."

Sky Sports is committed to making skysports.com and our channels on social media platforms a place for comment and debate that is free of abuse, hate and profanity.

If you see a reply to Sky Sports posts and/or content with an expression of hate on the basis of race, sex, colour, gender, nationality, ethnicity, disability, religion, sexuality, age or class, please copy the URL to the hateful post and screengrab it and email us here .

articles.title: Ireland Rugby Social: Jack Conan on Farrell's influence and desire to keep playing
articles.summary: Jack Conan tells the Ireland Rugby Social podcast of Andy Farrell's influence in implementing a cultural shift in camp, his shoulder injury and desire to keep playing while he feels physically and mentally able.
articles.body:
Ireland back row Jack Conan has praised head coach Andy Farrell for implementing a culture shift in camp to encourage players to talk more about their feelings.

Conan, who has won 62 caps since his Irish debut in 2015, has spent the majority of his international career working with Farrell, who was promoted to the head coach role in 2019 after working as a defence coach during Joe Schmidt's reign.

Conan believes Farrell's approach to open communication since he was appointed head coach has brought the squad closer together and helped new players settle quicker.

"He says 'I want you to be open and say how you are feeling whether it's good or bad, no wrong answers'," Conan told the Ireland Rugby Social podcast .

"I think when you are vulnerable or open it lets someone else be the same and it builds connection. I think it's been a real strong quality of the squad.

"Before, you'd be nervous and rattled and you wouldn't want to share [feelings] with anyone publicly in [team] meetings.

"Now, Faz would say 'do you all understand?' and people say now 'I don't' or 'I'm not sure'. You always fear being wrong to some degree, but if you have the best intentions and make a mistake it's fine. It's been a huge thing."

Conan sustained a shoulder injury in Leinster's Champions Cup win over Clermont earlier this month and will miss Ireland's November Nations Championship games against Argentina, Fiji and South Africa in Dublin.

The Bray native, who is a two-time British and Irish Lion, is aiming to be back and available for selection for next year's Six Nations and is desperate to feature at the 2027 Rugby World Cup next October.

His mother Ann died in August and Conan is striving to get back to fitness and enjoy his rugby to honour her memory.

"She used to text me before every single game and say 'good luck, we're proud'. That's all she ever said," a visibly emotional Conan said.

"That's a big thing for me now, enjoy it and make her proud. Take the stresses as a good thing and that's what I want to do."

While the 34-year-old acknowledges he is in the twilight years of his career, he feels physically and mentally able to carry on for the foreseeable future and will only start to consider retirement when he feels he has lost that edge to keep going.

"Bar the injury, my body feels good. As I'm getting older, I'm not getting weaker. I was never unbelievably quick, so physically I'm not declining, I'm still strong," he explained.

"I think when you get a little bit older, it's do you still really want it? Do you have it in you to show up on the hard days? Sometimes rehabbing now when I'm on a bike, I'm staring down the barrel and those are the real challenging moments.

"I still love what I do and the environment so that's what motivates you. Whether I play one, two or three years, we'll have to wait and see but right now I feel good and that doggedness is still there.

"I get a bit sick other lads are playing - it spurs me on which I think is healthy. I still want to compete."

articles.title: Ireland v Argentina: Craig Casey, Nick Timoney and Sean Jansen all to start against Pumas
articles.summary: Nick Timoney, Craig Casey and Sean Jansen will start for Ireland against Argentina in the Nations Championship on Friday night with Jamison Gibson-Park and Josh van der Flier on the bench at the Aviva Stadium.
articles.body:
Nick Timoney, Craig Casey and Sean Jansen will start for Ireland against Argentina in the Nations Championship on Friday night, with Jamison Gibson-Park and Josh van der Flier on the bench at Aviva Stadium.

With captain Caelan Doris and two-tour British and Irish Lion Jack Conan missing through injury, Connacht's Jansen always seemed the most likely to fill in at number eight for head coach Andy Farrell.

The 27-year-old made a try-scoring debut for Ireland against Japan in July and followed that with a cameo as a replacement against the All Blacks a week later.

The selections of Casey and Timoney, however, were less expected.

Influential scrum-half Gibson-Park has arguably been Ireland's best performer in recent seasons.

The 34-year-old missed the start of Leinster's season with a groin injury but made his return in the win over Munster on 24 October.

With only that game under his belt this season, he will start on the bench with Casey preferred to start at nine in a half-back partnership with fly-half Sam Prendergast, who has recovered from a wrist injury.

Ulster back row Timoney, 31, previously struggled to regularly break into the side despite strong form for his province, but selection against Argentina means he will be involved in his ninth consecutive Test.

Seven of those appearances, however, have been from the bench and his start on Friday night comes at the expense of former World Rugby player of the year Van der Flier.

Live commentary on BBC Radio Ulster, BBC Sport website and app

With Garry Ringrose ruled out because of a hamstring problem, the experienced Robbie Henshaw will wear the 13 jersey, forming a midfield partnership with Stuart McCloskey.

Wing Mack Hansen, prop Andrew Porter and Ryan Baird all start, having not featured for Ireland since the defeat by South Africa in November 2025.

All three missed the Six Nations and summer fixtures in the Nations Championship through injury.

Hansen starts in the number 11 jersey in what is Ireland's first home game since James Lowe's departure from Irish rugby, with Robert Baloucoune keeping his spot on the right wing and Hugo Keenan selected at full-back.

Baird is selected at blind-side flanker, joining Timoney and Jansen in the back row.

Porter's return at loose-head will be a considerable boost for coach Farrell after recent windows were impact by injury problems at the position.

He will pack down alongside hooker Dan Sheehan, who captains the side in Doris' absence, and tight-head Tadhg Furlong.

Furlong is free to play after he was cleared by a disciplinary committee of grabbing Gavin Coombes in the groin last month.

With Tadhg Beirne and Joe McCarthy selected as starting locks, James Ryan must make do with a place on the bench alongside Van der Flier and Gibson-Park.

Sam Illo, who will make his home debut if called upon, Ronan Kelleher, Tom O'Toole, Ciaran Frawley and Bundee Aki are Ireland's other replacements.

Argentina boss Felipe Contepomi has made 12 changes from the side that drew 28-28 with Australia in September as Los Pumas seek a first away win over Ireland.

Toulouse full-back Juan Cruz Mallia returns to win a first cap since November 2025 after injury.

Ireland: Hugo Keenan; Robert Baloucoune, Robbie Henshaw, Stuart McCloskey, Mack Hansen; Sam Prendergast, Craig Casey; Andrew Porter, Dan Sheehan (capt), Tadhg Furlong; Joe McCarthy, Tadhg Beirne; Ryan Baird, Nick Timoney, Sean Jansen.

Replacements: Ronan Kelleher, Tom O'Toole, Sam Illo, James Ryan, Josh van der Flier, Jamison Gibson-Park, Ciaran Frawley or Jamie Benson, Bundee Aki.

Argentina: Juan Cruz Mallia; Bautista Delguy, Justo Piccardo, Santiago Chocobares, Mateo Carreras; Tomas Albornoz, Gonzalo Garcia; Boris Wenger, Julian Montoya (capt), Francisco Moreno; Guido Petti, Pedro Rubiolo; Juan Martin Gonzalez, Marcos Kremer, Pablo Matera.

Replacements: Leonel Oviedo, Mayco Vivas, Joel Sclavi, Efrain Elias, Juan Martin Scelzo, Simon Benitez Cruz, Geronimo Prisciantelli, Lucio Cinti.
